item.title: House Democrats are fearful of all the ways impeaching Trump could go wrong
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A growing number of House Democrats say they’re open to using their new majority to impeach President Donald Trump — but they’re concerned that a rush job could backfire. After two attempts to remove the president during the first Trump administration, many members are heeding advice from colleagues who led those previous battles and say a third attempt must be methodical or risk playing into the weakened president’s hands. “I think Donald Trump would love us to organize a campaign of impeachment against him right now because he thinks that's his last hope for rallying the dwindling MAGA base at this point,” said Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who is poised to lead the House Judiciary Committee next year and ran the impeachment trial against Trump over the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol. Indeed, Trump has previously declared that his first two impeachments benefited him politically and said recently he would welcome the prospect of a third. “I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did that, because it would be impeachment for no reason,” he said to reporters a day after the GOP’s midterm drubbing . “For what? For having a successful country?” Trump’s comment hits on another fundamental dilemma for Democrats: What, precisely, would a new round of impeachment articles against Trump say? While Democrats have accused him of wide-ranging corruption — self-enrichment, accepting foreign gifts, granting pay-for-play pardons, abusing power to target his enemies and launching an illegal war in Iran — there is no consensus about what charges a Democratic House would level, or what type of investigation would precede formal action. Interviews with 14 House Democrats from across the ideological spectrum reveal a desire to proceed with varying degrees of caution as party leaders plot the next two years in power ahead of the next presidential election, when Trump will be term-limited out of office anyway. Some Democrats say the chamber should prioritize policy fights rather than impeachment — including Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.) who led the now-defunct Jan. 6 committee that concluded Trump presented a unique danger to the republic. “Impeachment is not a priority for me,” said Thompson, the likely next chair of the Homeland Security committee. “If other members file a resolution and it gets to the floor, I'll vote for it.” Many Democrats worry that dragging the country through divisive and time-consuming impeachment proceedings could prove futile if they don’t first lay the groundwork to persuade the public that such an exercise is necessary. And even a perfectly executed process would run into a math problem: It takes two-thirds of the Senate to convict a president in an impeachment trial, meaning Democrats would need at least 11 Republicans to join them for a conviction — a threshold they failed to clear even in the days after the Jan. 6 riot. Raskin noted the tricky “constitutional arithmetic,” and he’s not alone. “Is the Senate going to convict? You need to weigh that in and whether to proceed,” said Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.), who served with Thompson and Raskin on the Jan. 6 committee. She was also an impeachment manager in 2020, when Democrats sought to remove Trump on grounds he threatened to withhold foreign aid to Ukraine unless president Volodymyr Zelenskyy agreed to investigate his political enemies. “I think we need a national conversation,” Lofgren added. Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) was even more blunt: “No,” he said when asked whether the House should impeach Trump. “I'm a former prosecutor. You don't indict somebody if you don't think you can convict.” Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be speaker in January and was himself a manager in the Ukraine-related impeachment trial, has so far taken a cautious approach to the issue. “I haven't had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment,” Jeffries said a day after the midterms. “We've been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability.” When asked Thursday if Trump has committed impeachable offenses, Jeffries dodged: “As I've repeatedly indicated, we haven't ruled anything in. We haven't ruled anything out. We're going to follow the facts. We're going to apply the law. We're going to be guided by the Constitution, and we're going to let the chips fall where they may.” Jeffries’ approach tracks closely with that of his predecessor Nancy Pelosi, who as speaker resisted early pressure from Democrats to rush toward impeachment after they took the majority in 2019. Though some members were then eager to impeach Trump over allegations stemming from the investigation of his contacts with Russia, Pelosi insisted that the chamber wait to build a clear case to the public that impeachment was warranted. Her calculus changed when a whistleblower informed Congress about Trump’s dealings with Zelenskyy. Some Democratic lawmakers are convinced that Trump’s penchant for escalation against his adversaries could give them fresh fodder for impeachment in the next Congress. “We'll see what the next two years bring in terms of what Trump does,” said Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) in an interview. “Because I also do worry that he's going to get more and more desperate and more and more volatile, and who knows what actions he may take that just become impossible to ignore when it comes to impeachment.” But Ansari also acknowledged the potential for a strategic blunder in rushing headlong into the process: “I am torn on it. I believe that he should be impeached, but I also hear the concerns of colleagues, especially ones who were here and have been through that. That perhaps that would suck the oxygen in a way that is not the most effective.” Another deterrent for Democrats: A quick impeachment in the House would trigger a Senate trial that would grind Washington to a halt, just as Democrats are attempting to make good on their promises to prioritize affordability for Americans. Presidential impeachments instantly displace other Senate business and even typically requires the chief justice of the Supreme Court to preside. At the same time, Democratic leaders will also have to deal with a faction that remains driven to impeach Trump quickly, who argue that slow-walking proceedings in the face of impeachable offenses would be risky in a different way. “It's setting a dangerous precedent when people [are] like, ‘no, it's a distraction.’ What are you talking about?” said Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.), who famously rankled party leaders by declaring her intent to “impeach the motherfucker” just days after taking office in 2019. “This won't be the last president that runs businesses out of the Oval Office.” Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) also said Democrats shouldn’t be afraid to stand their ground: “If there is something that is worthy of impeachment, we should have impeachment, even if it's bad politics.” Democrats also need to be attuned to voters who may want to see the party hold Trump accountable, said Rep. Becca Balint (D-Vt.), while noting she would vote for an impeachment resolution on the floor. “There's definitely a core of our base that wants revenge and vengeance, right? And there's another group, actually, that just wants to make sure that the Constitution will hold, and that they feel like if [Trump] is allowed to get away with this without a third impeachment, then what does that say about the system?” she said in an interview. Ultimately, Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.), who served as a manager in Trump’s first trial, said it was important to remember that impeachment is just one option for holding the president accountable. “Impeachment has taken on this almost mythical place in American culture because people know about it. But it's a tool. It's not an end in and of itself,” he said. “I've done it before … and if I thought that was appropriate, I would do it again. But right now, we have to see what type of coalition we can put together.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/16/trump-impeachment-house-democrats-strategy-01166649

item.title: Trump says he may meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un during China trip
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. As he departed the White House Monday morning, Trump said he "may" meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China as well, though he said it would ultimately be Xi's decision. "He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump said of Kim Jong Un. KCNA/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un speaks during a conference of company commanders for North Korea's Army, in Pyongyang, North Korea, in this picture released by North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency, October 24, 2026. Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, senior U.S. officials said. The president is expected to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, he does not intend to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting, officials say. Trump to meet with Putin and Xi in China next week, US officials say Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials said they do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject. Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization. Reuters/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: Chinese President Xi Jinping Beijing, November 12, 2026, President Donald Trump in Washington, November 9, 2026 and Russia's President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, November 12, 2026. Trump and Xi will have a bilateral meeting ahead of the trilateral, though Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said. The president's trip comes as questions linger about what the administration knew about prominent tech CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels. Officials did not specify his reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to Musk's business interests in China. An official said they expect some additional U.S. business leaders to be attending the APEC CEO Summit, but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation. Breakdown of the trip Trump is expected to leave Washington in the morning of Monday, Nov. 16 and arrive in Manila in the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17, and will head to a bilateral meeting with the other members of the Quad, a diplomatic partnership the U.S. has with Australia, India, and Japan, about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand. He will then participate in an ASEAN cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner. The next day, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony at Malacañang Presidential Palace, the official residence of Filipino President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Romualdez Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. He will also participate in an Association of Southeast Asian Nations cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner. After Wednesday’s events in the Philippines, Trump travels to Shenzhen, China, where it is expected that a minister will greet Trump on the tarmac. He will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon local time, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Chinese President Xi. Maxim Shemetov/Reuters - PHOTO: Chinese President Xi Jinping looks on during a meeting commemorating the 160th anniversary of birth of Sun Yat-sen at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, China, November 12, 2026. The historic trilateral Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia swing. Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy Each of Trump and Xi’s meetings this year have been clouded by other topics. When Trump visited China in May, the raging war in Iran overshadowed the state visit that was scheduled after a detente in Trump's tit-for-tat trade war. Also, when Trump welcomed Xi in September, the pomp and circumstance Trump had planned went without live TV coverage after his banning outlets from the press pool led to a network boycott. Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: President Donald Trump speaks with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence in the East Room of the White House in Washington, September 29, 2026. Now, in the background of this trip, is the scandal involving Nvidia's CEO, Huang, who joined Trump's last trip to China earlier this year after boarding Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, according to pool reports at the time. Huang was reported to have had an affair with Alice Huang , a Chinese national and tech executive who is accused of being a Chinese spy. Officials said they do not expect Trump to raise the allegations against Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, with President Xi, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement. "You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said. Timeline of the stunning fall of powerful Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Huang resigned from Nvidia's board and as its president and CEO on Nov. 12. This scandal engulfing Huang has introduced scrutiny over Trump’s ties to him and what Trump and other administration officials knew about the relationship with the alleged spy. "Well, I've been hearing about it and I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference in the White House briefing room on Nov. 9. When pressed on if he was aware of the allegations during his May trip to China, Trump said: "No, I didn't hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that he had." On May 12, Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared intelligence with Trump on Air Force One showing Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the plot. Trump was briefed by Rubio shortly before Huang was set to join Trump on the trip to China, the U.S. official and sources said. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images - PHOTO: President Donald Trump, Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang walk back to the White House following a media briefing after a meeting on artificial intelligence outside the White House, Sept. 29, 2026 in Washington. A U.S. official and a source familiar with the matter told ABC News that after Air Force One landed in China, White House officials asked for business leaders -- including Huang -- to be allowed into a meeting with President Xi. Initially, the Chinese were hesitant to adjust the program, but ultimately agreed to it. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, one of the world’s most-valuable companies and the maker of chips that top AI companies heavily rely on, has been a constant presence around Trump, who has invited tech executives to multiple events, both at the White House and on overseas trips. Since April 28, when Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a state dinner for King Charles III and Queen Camila, the tech CEO has participated in at least six events with Trump, including the September state dinner for Xi. Huang has lobbied for policy positions that benefit China and Chinese companies over the past few months. House and Senate Republicans call on Howard Lutnick, Jensen Huang to testify about Nvidia For example, the U.S. has long blocked China's access to American AI chips. However, in December 2025, after lobbying from Huang, Trump loosened those restrictions -- approving the sale of some older but still powerful chips to China as part of a remarkable deal that gave the U.S. government a 25% cut of the sales. And in July of this year, Huang joined the social media platform X to push back against possible bans on open-weight AI models, the type that Chinese companies have embraced, and which would be cheaper for businesses and governments to adopt. The ban would benefit American companies OpenAI and Anthropic, which use closed models. The U.S. was reportedly considering those bans. "The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models," Huang wrote in his first-ever X post. Midterms This trip marks Trump's first one overseas since American voters handed him and Republicans a devastating defeat in the midterm elections. Voter Polls show voters rejected the president’s tariffs and the war in Iran -- two of Trump's key foreign policy positions. Trump says 'too tough' deportation policies hurt him in the midterms The tariffs have been ensnared in legal challenges in count -- and Democrats, who will take the majority in January, have vowed to counter them and reassert congressional authority over trade. They don’t have a veto-proof majority, however, and Trump has vowed to use his veto pen to kill bills he doesn't like. And the president does not appear to feel pressure to reign in his sweeping tariffs. On Nov. 12, he threatened to double tariffs on Mexico if they don't stop what he claims are caravans heading to the southern border post-midterms. This article originally appeared on Good Morning America at https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-heads-asia-2nd-high-stakes-meeting-chinese/story?id=138059807

item.title: DOJ official warns Sen. Warren against investigating Trump's allies
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The letter to Warren signals an expansion of Reitz’s inquiry into congressional Democrats tasked with government oversight. (Al Drago / Bloomberg via Getty) A Justice Department official on Sunday accused Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., of intending to target private individuals close to President Donald Trump with investigations. The complaint came in a letter similar to others sent to congressional Democrats. U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz sent a letter to Warren — who is likely the incoming chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee — calling on her to preserve documents related to investigations of Trump allies. Reitz noted that Warren appears “eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates.” Reitz referenced a Nov. 11 letter in which Warren, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., asked Meredith O’Rourke, a National Park Foundation board member and top fundraiser for Trump, to retain documents related to funding for the White House ballroom and other projects. Reitz accused the three lawmakers of “demanding sweeping information about her and other private citizens and entities who associate with President Trump.” The letter to Warren signals an expansion of Reitz’s inquiry into congressional Democrats tasked with government oversight. When Democrats take control of Congress next year, Garcia is likely to take the gavel of the House Oversight Committee, while Blumenthal is expected to lead the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs’ Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. Last week, the White House issued a threat to congressional Democrats against probes into the administration. Since their midterm victories, Democrats have said Trump family businesses and immigration enforcement are some of their top targets for investigation. Reitz’s letter referenced an op-ed from Warren earlier this month in Time magazine, in which the senator wrote, “With astonishing brazenness, Trump has attempted to reengineer the federal government into a corruption machine designed to rake in profits for himself, his family, and his cronies.” Reitz also accused Warren of planning to target businesses that associate with Trump, referencing an appearance on CBS’ “Face the Nation” in which Warren said tech CEOs, Wall Street executives and giant corporations who have broken the law “better get ready for some investigations — serious ones.” “The context sends a strong smoke signal: you intend to target private individuals close to President Trump,” Reitz said. A spokesperson for Warren did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday night. Reitz, a former chief of staff to Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has sent similar letters to Blumenthal and Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., warning them against investigating Trump associates and calling on them to preserve documents. Reitz posted his letter to Warren on X, and Trump reposted it to Truth Social later Sunday. The letter to Warren also contained numerous references to Native Americans, such as “scalps,” “war cries” and “tomahawk,” a dig at Warren over her past claims of Native American descent. This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/us-attorney-warns-sen-elizabeth-warren-investigating-trump-associates-rcna609532

item.title: Jensen Huang allies assemble 'war room' in attempt to return ex-Nvidia CEO to his post
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock fell 4% on Monday as investors weighed tighter US restrictions on overseas access to advanced AI semiconductors and a report that supporters of Jensen Huang are lobbying for his return to the chip heavyweight following his abrupt resignation last week. Huang has discussed returning as CEO with confidants, the Financial Times reported Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter. Huang resigned last week following reports of affairs, including one with a woman who was reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy. According to the report, a Huang supporter said that a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives was being assembled to lobby Nvidia's board to reinstate him, including by seeking support from the White House. "Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen," the person said, adding that Huang supported the effort. On Monday, CNBC reported that the board was not considering bringing Huang back to the company. Meanwhile, SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) CEO Elon Musk has come out in support of Huang, writing on X last Friday , "A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen, and I'm signing it too." On Saturday, Musk said , "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract. Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost." The push to bring Huang back comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's board had approached Arm Holdings ( ARM ) CEO Rene Haas as it searches for a successor. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO during the search. Yorkville's Dan Ives said that while no “one individual can replace Jensen as CEO," any talk of "Jensen coming back to Nvidia is ridiculous in our view given the legal/Board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles." Huang abruptly stepped down Thursday following reports of alleged affairs with a former executive from Singapore-based Megaspeed, and also an Nvidia employee who reported directly to him. Days earlier, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife but did not disclose how many affairs he had or identify those involved. Recent reports have raised concerns about whether restricted semiconductors were being diverted to China and if sensitive US information had been sent to Beijing. The developments have also sent shockwaves through the AI industry, where Nvidia has played a central role in building the ecosystem. The company has become a bellwether for the AI trade and has invested in key parts of the industry, including large language model development, energy, optics, and cloud providers. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results Tuesday after the bell in what will be the company's first earnings call without Huang. Nvidia stock declined more than 12% last week, closing below a $4 trillion market cap. At least 10 Wall Street analysts have recently downgraded the stock from Buy to Hold, with many citing, in part, increased scrutiny in Washington and succession uncertainty. This article originally appeared on Yahoo Finance at https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/nvidia-stock-steady-as-jensen-huang-reportedly-weighs-ceo-comeback-musk-backs-return-015644730.html

item.title: Poll shows that 35% of Trump voters skipped the midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump (AP) New survey results show that 35% of President Donald Trump's 2024 voters didn't cast a ballot in the midterm elections. The findings suggest Republicans' crushing losses this month were driven largely by Trump supporters staying home rather than abandoning the GOP for Democrats, according to a new J.L. Partners analysis reported by the New York Post . The pollster found that low Republican turnout accounted for 10 percentage points of the 15-point swing toward Democrats since 2024, while voters switching parties accounted for the remaining five points. Just 8% of Trump's 2024 supporters voted for Democrats on Nov. 3. "The GOP should not throw the MAGA baby out with the bathwater just yet," J.L. Partners founding director James Johnson said, the Post reported. "If Republicans can energize their 2024 vote in 2028, then they may yet have a shot at winning again." The analysis, based on an Election Day survey of 1,000 registered voters and more than 30,000 campaign interviews, found particularly steep turnout declines among key segments of Trump's coalition. Among his 2024 supporters, 46% of those without college degrees failed to vote, along with 44% of those older than 65 and 39% of rural voters. Johnson said the turnout collapse alone would have cost Republicans control of Congress, even without voters switching parties. "Even without a single voter switching, the GOP would have lost the Senate and House," Johnson said. The findings bolster Trump's argument that Republicans suffered because he wasn't on the ballot. However, Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis suggested GOP voters stayed home because they were dissatisfied with congressional Republicans' performance. "A lot of our voters who stayed home, they stayed home because they were frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate," DeSantis told Fox News. The survey also found potential vulnerabilities for Democrats heading into 2028. Nearly half of Democrat voters, 48%, said their midterm vote was primarily against Trump rather than in support of Democrat policies. Only 30% of registered voters believed Democrats have a viable presidential candidate for 2028. Meanwhile, CNN reported that Trump's declining popularity remains a significant obstacle for Republicans. CNN's voter polling found that 86% of Americans who disapproved of Trump's performance backed Democrats in House races. Cost of living emerged as the leading concern across every demographic group in the J.L. Partners survey. Johnson suggested the Iran war contributed to voter frustration over rising prices, particularly gasoline. The survey's overall margin of error was 3.4 percentage points. Despite the GOP's losses, Johnson said the results indicate Republicans could rebound by rebuilding turnout among Trump's 2024 supporters rather than abandoning the political coalition that returned him to the White House. © 2026 Newsmax. All rights reserved.This article originally appeared on Newsmax at https://www.newsmax.com/politics/poll-donald-trump-voters/2026/11/16/id/1276447

item.title: Mayor Mamdani to disband controversial NYPD protest unit, fulfilling promise
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch have agreed to disband the department's Strategic Response Group, or SRG, after months of discussions, officials announced Monday. "What we're doing today is announcing the disbanding of the Strategic Response Group and announcing a completely new approach to how we treat protest in our city," Mamdani told Eyewitness News in an exclusive joint interview with the NYPD Commissioner. The SRG is the NYPD's citywide rapid-deployment force that specializes in counterterrorism but also responds to major crimes and mass demonstrations. Critics have argued that the unit's crowd-control tactics are heavy-handed and provocative. Tisch said the SRG's 500 highly trained, uniformed officers will be reassigned, with many moving to the department's Counterterrorism Bureau. When asked whether the move represented a compromise, Tisch said, "No, I would never compromise on security for New Yorkers. And over the past year, we have made a number of massive changes in the department that strengthen our counterterrorism efforts, this among them." Mamdani said the city's new approach will focus on reducing tensions during demonstrations. "In addition to separating out those responsibilities, we're also emphasizing an approach of de-escalation, an approach of dialogue," he said. Over the next year, the city plans to hire and train civilians to work with protest organizers before and during demonstrations. Tisch said the change will not affect how the NYPD responds to civil disorder. "Nothing would change about the way that the NYPD responds to crowd control conditions, like, for example, the celebrations following the Knicks' epic championship," Tisch said. "And so New Yorkers can expect in crowd control type situations to see the very same response that they are accustomed to." Disbanding the SRG was one of Mamdani's campaign promises. The unit is scheduled to be dissolved in the spring of next year, when a new NYPD crowd-control unit will assume responsibility for facilitating nonviolent protests. See more of N.J. FAST will handle dialogue and de-escalation while CDDD is being built. Creates New Patrol Unit: Establishesthe Patrol SupportDivision, which reports to the Patrol Services Bureau and will comprise vetted officers who will receive specialized training and conduct arrests at protests in rare instances, if necessary. PSD will work with CDDD and FAST when respondingtoFirstAmendment activities, building on the reforms agreed to in the Payne Protest Settlement. For the vast majority of the time, PSD will serve as a resource to patrol, including participating in searches for missing persons, supporting major events, such as the NYC Marathon and Thanksgiving Day Parade, and assisting with priority traffic posts during hazardous weather. There will be strict eligibility requirements to enter the PSD. Regulates aggressive crowd-management tactics: Codifies the ban on kettling, prohibits the use of long guns and tear gas during First Amendment activities and limits long-range acoustic devices to 90 decibels. Pepper spray will not be used as a general crowd-management device. These reforms will be implemented at no additional cost and without increasing or reducing NYPD headcount. item.title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial in March over killing of her children
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Lindsay Clancy will face a retrial in March 2027 in connection with the deaths of her three children, a Massachusetts judge ruled Monday, after a jury failed to reach a verdict in her first trial earlier this year. Judge William Sullivan set March 29 as the date for a second trial during a status hearing Monday. Prosecutors sought a May trial date, citing other cases on the docket, but Sullivan, who is retiring in June 2027, was firm on setting it for March in Plymouth Superior Court. Prosecutors didn't explicitly say during Monday's hearing that they would pursue first-degree murder charges again, but they indicated to Sullivan that a jury would be needed for the trial. Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, said the need for a jury indicates that prosecutors plan to seek first-degree murder charges again, Reuters reported. If prosecutors sought to convict Clancy on second-degree murder charges, she would have the option to waive a jury trial and potentially have the case heard by a judge. The judge's decision came a week after he rejected the defense's motion to dismiss the murder charges against Clancy. Sullivan ruled that a second trial would not violate Clancy's constitutional protection against double jeopardy. The Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial on Sept. 4 after a single holdout juror prevented the 12-member jury from reaching a unanimous decision on whether she was criminally responsible for her actions. Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse, admitted to strangling her children — Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan — at their Duxbury, Mass., home in January 2023. However, her lawyers argued that she could not be held criminally responsible because she had a rare mental illness — postpartum psychosis — that they said prevented her from understanding the wrongfulness of her actions. Prosecutors contended that Clancy, who had not been formally diagnosed with postpartum psychosis before the killings, carefully planned them and bears full responsibility for her children's deaths. Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside of Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 20, 2026. John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images The trial hinged largely on discussions of Clancy's mental state. Over nearly five weeks of testimony, a series of family members and medical professionals took the stand to describe the mental and emotional struggles she experienced in the months leading up to the killings. The prosecution and defense are set to return to court on Dec. 30, 2026, at 9 a.m. ET to sort out trial logistics, security and media arrangements, according to the Associated Press . A pretrial conference is scheduled for Feb. 18, 2027. item.title: Blanche chides 'incoming freshmen' Democrats for 'acting like prosecutors'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday blasted "incoming freshmen" Democrats who were elected in the 2026 midterm elections for "acting like prosecutors" in joining lawmakers' calls to open investigations into President Trump and his administration. Fox News host Mark Levin asked Blanche on his show " Life, Liberty & Levin " if Congress can act "like a judiciary and an executive prosecutorial operation." "No, that's exactly right," Blanche answered. "And what you've heard, these incoming freshmen, and some of them are brand new to Congress –– so hopefully they'll learn –– is they're acting like prosecutors. They're acting like they're going to cut subpoenas left and right, and they're going to investigate, and they're going to have a trial and a conviction, and that's absolutely not their job." Blanche said Democrats can conduct oversight, "but that's not the rhetoric we're hearing right now from these guys." He later added that he hopes it's only rhetoric and that they will "actually try to do their job, try to work with President Trump. Like he said, he would work with them." But should Democrats open investigations, "we're going to be there and we're not going to just stand by willingly and let them destroy their function, and we're not going to let that happen." "They said 'lawyer up,'" Blanche said, referring to remarks made by incoming House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) shortly after the midterms. "You only lawyer up if you're concerned there's going to be some kind of criminal investigation." Blanche also referred to comments Garcia made last week saying that White House chief of staff Stephen Miller "should be preserving documents" before the new Congress starts. "They went after the chief of staff for the president of the United States without saying anything he did wrong," the attorney general noted. "Because he's done nothing wrong except to work hard for the American people, work hard for President Trump." "And again, I have –– I really have hope this rhetoric stops, but unfortunately, I'm not optimistic given what they've said in the past two weeks, but maybe they'll change their tune before January," Blanche continued. Garcia's comment reverberated among other Democratic lawmakers who are calling to investigate alleged corruption and continue probes into Trump's ties to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and the activities carried out by the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency at the start of Trump's second term. White House counsel Will Scharf clapped back at Garcia last week, writing in a letter that the administration will consider whether the investigations and subsequent subpoenas could amount to criminal activity . "We’re going to see what happens in January, but we’re ready to fight tooth and nail here if that’s the road they want to go down," Scharf later said on Newsmax. Some Democratic lawmakers responded by saying the administration was hiding things involving the president in connection with their vows to conduct oversight. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) said Scharf's reply to Garcia was "an act of desperation" and that Democratic lawmakers "should not be afraid of them." Other Democrats were defiant, with Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.) responding, " Come at me, bro ." Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed.
